problem.text: The KNRS conjecture for subdivisions of graphs, and its consequences for Sidorenko's conjecture.

claims.text: Theorem 1.4: if H is KNRS, then every odd subdivision H^(2k-1) is Sidorenko and every even subdivision H^(2k) is weakly-KNRS. Theorem 1.5: if H is KNRS and regular, then H^(2k) is KNRS. Corollary 1.6: balanced subdivisions of regular KNRS graphs, in particular of cliques, are KNRS.

assumptions.text: The host may be taken d-regular (Lemma 2.2, from Coregliano and Razborov, Theorem 8.2); the KNRS property is used in its graphon form for d-locally dense graphons (Lemma 2.3, from Bradač, Sudakov and Wigderson), with the weighted Reiher inequality (Lemmas 2.8 and 2.9).

methods.text: t(H^(s), W) = t(H, W_{s+1}) for the path kernel W_{s+1} (Lemma 3.1); for a d-regular W the even path kernel W_{2k} is d^{2k}-locally dense by Cauchy-Schwarz, and the KNRS property of H finishes Theorem 1.4(a); restrictions to closed sets and a normalized kernel give Theorems 1.4(b) and 1.5.

evidence.text: Complete proofs, with an appendix for the restriction lemma.

limitations.text: Every result needs the base graph to be KNRS, and few non-bipartite graphs are known to be KNRS. The authors cannot show that even subdivisions of KNRS graphs are KNRS without regularity, and they ask whether weakly-KNRS graphs are KNRS.

relevance.text: No result of this paper decides the girth-six statement. Theorem 1.4(a) gives special cases of the statement: an odd subdivision H^(2k-1) of a KNRS graph H has girth at least 6k, so it is a Sidorenko graph of girth at least six. For the 1-subdivision of an arbitrary graph (Conlon, Kim, Lee and Lee, Problem 1.5, a declared neighbour) the route of Conlon, Kim, Lee and Lee and of this paper needs the base graph to be KNRS, and the KNRS property is open for most non-bipartite graphs. The paper names K_{5,5} minus a 10-cycle as the smallest open case of Sidorenko's conjecture; that graph is cubic, bipartite and has 10 vertices, so it has a 4-cycle (the smallest cubic graph of girth six, the Heawood graph, has 14 vertices) and is outside the class of the statement.
